title: Gaikwad Scored a Hundred. Sooryavanshi Scored Fourteen. In Dambulla, the Old Hand Had the Answers.
excerpt: At 17 for 2 in the tri-series opener against Sri Lanka A, India A needed steadiness, not stardom. Ruturaj Gaikwad delivered both.
body:
The fifteen-year-old everyone came to watch scored 14 off 12 balls. The twenty-seven-year-old nobody was talking about scored a hundred. In Dambulla on Monday, the India A tri-series opener against Sri Lanka A was supposed to be the Vaibhav Sooryavanshi show. It turned into a Ruturaj Gaikwad masterclass.

Tilak Varma won the toss and chose to bat at the Rangiri Dambulla International Stadium. Sooryavanshi, opening alongside Prabhsimran Singh, announced himself with three boundaries in his first twelve deliveries — a flicked four, a driven four, and another through the off-side that bore the signature aggression of his IPL 2026 campaign. Then Mohammad Shiraz got one to hold its line, Sooryavanshi tried to clear mid-off without getting enough elevation, and Sahan Arachchige dived forward to take the catch.

The prodigy was gone. The questions were coming. Could a fifteen-year-old who scored 776 runs at a strike rate of 237 in T20 cricket adapt to the 50-over game?

## From Crisis to Control

At 17 for 2, with Prabhsimran Singh also dismissed cheaply for 2 off 11 balls, India A were teetering. Priyansh Arya and Gaikwad steadied the ship, adding 52 for the third wicket before a bizarre run-out — both batters on the same side after a miscommunication — sent Arya back for 32 off 32 balls.

That brought Varma to the crease at 69 for 3, and from that point, the character of the innings changed entirely. Gaikwad, the Chennai Super Kings captain who has averaged over 50 in List A cricket, found his rhythm. He was unhurried through the first thirty overs, reaching his fifty off 65 balls with a mix of elegant drives and calculated nudges.

Then he accelerated. After his half-century, the boundaries came in clusters — a punched four past a diving mid-on off Chamika Karunaratne, pull shots that bisected the deep fielders, and cuts off the back foot that raced to the boundary. By the time he brought up his century, the innings had shifted from survival to dominance.

Varma, India's T20I vice-captain and the man being groomed for leadership across formats, contributed a disciplined fifty. Their partnership rebuilt the innings completely, transforming 69 for 3 into a competitive 277 for 6 at the close of India A's 50 overs.

## The Bigger Picture

This tri-series — featuring India A, Sri Lanka A, and Afghanistan A — exists to answer questions. Can Sooryavanshi play the long game? Is Tilak Varma ready to lead? Can Gaikwad force his way back into the senior ODI side after being overlooked since his maiden hundred against South Africa?

One match does not answer all of them. But Gaikwad's century makes a statement that selectors will find hard to ignore. With India's ODI squad for the Afghanistan series already announced and the England tour looming in July, the competition for batting spots is fierce. Gaikwad's response was the most eloquent kind — a hundred when his team needed it, on a surface that was not easy for batting, in a format where patience matters more than pyrotechnics.

Sooryavanshi's 14 off 12 was a glimpse, not a verdict. The teenager showed intent with three fours in his brief stay, and the shot that got him out — an attempted loft over mid-off — was the kind of attacking instinct that makes him special. In T20 cricket, that goes for six. In 50-over cricket, the margin for error shrinks. He will learn. He is fifteen.

## What It Means for NRIs

For the Indian diaspora following cricket across time zones, the tri-series is easy to miss. It is not on the main broadcast channels in most markets, and the A-team fixtures rarely make headlines. But these are the games where India's next generation is being forged.

Gaikwad is twenty-seven. He has led CSK in the IPL. He has scored hundreds in white-ball cricket at the international level. Yet he keeps being told to wait. His century in Dambulla is a reminder that waiting has limits, and that form, eventually, demands opportunity.
